Kid got game.

The game:

![Genius Square Game Gox. Source: [goldersgames.co.uk](https://www.goldersgames.co.uk/the-genius-square)](genius-square-box.jpg)

In the game and on the link above, they say:

> There are 62,208 possible combinations in which the dice can fall. Using a specially devised computer programme, we have confirmed that all of them have at least one possible solution. Some combinations will be easy to solve, some much harder. It’s all in the luck of the roll of the dice.

As a coder myself, my ears perked up at the mention of a "specially devised computer programme" and I wanted to see what it takes to make that confirmation myself. One of the first things to do was take a look at the dice.

## The Dice

The board is 6×6 and there are 7 pegs with a 6-sided die for each one. 36 grid ids are distributed across 42 die faces, so there have to be 6 duplicate faces. Take a look at how those duplicates are distributed:

| Die | Face 1 | Face 2 | Face 3 | Face 4 | Face 5 | Face 6 |
|-----|--------|--------|--------|--------|--------|--------|
| 1   | B4     | C3     | C4     | D3     | D4     | E3     |
| 2   | A2     | A3     | B1     | B2     | B3     | C2     |
| 3   | A4     | B5     | C5     | C6     | D6     | F6     |
| 4   | D5     | E4     | E5     | E6     | F4     | F5     |
| 5   | A1     | C1     | D1     | D2     | E2     | F3     |
| 6   | A5     | **A5** | B6     | E1     | F2     | **F2** |
| 7   | A6     | **A6** | **A6** | F1     | **F1** | **F1** |

The duplicate faces are in boldface above. What do you notice? That's right, they're packing all the duplicates into 2 dice! With this setup, the number of unique combinations is 6×6×6×6×6×4×2=62,208 as advertised. But if they had spread the duplicates out with one duplicate face on each of 6 dice, we could have had 5×5×5×5×5×5×6=93,750 combinations! They're shorting us a whopping 34% of the possible combinations we could have had.

On the bright side, it could have been worse. If they made all the faces of one die the same grid id, we would only have had 6×6×6×6×6×5×1=38,880 combinations. But still, why deprive us of tens of thousands of combinations? Is it that hard to set ensure solvable puzzles with the max number of combinations? I had to get to the bottom of this important question.

## Total Peg Combinations

What's the total number of peg combinations we could have *without* the restriction of dice? Since we're looking at combinations of 7 pegs chosen from 36 spots where order doesn't matter, that's $C(36,7)=8,347,680$ (read "36 choose 7"). That's a lot more than a measly 93,750! Now how many of those combinations are solvable?

## Genius Square Solver

To figure that out, I'd need a genius square solver that is reasonably fast to power through all those combinations. If I can determine which puzzles are solvable and which aren't, we're one step closer to finding a better die face arrangement.

10000 solutions in about 1 minute. About 14 hours to evaluate all combos

With random rolls, 1000 solutions in 4 minutes. About 550 hours to evaluate all combos.
